item.title: Universal Short-Time Fourier Transform: Data-Adaptive Window-Length Selection for Time-Frequency Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.37795v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The short-time Fourier transform (STFT) characterizes the local frequency content of time-varying signals by evaluating the discrete Fourier transform over a sliding analysis window. The STFT is governed by a fundamental resolution trade-off: a short window localizes rapid transients in time at the cost of frequency resolution, whereas a long window resolves closely spaced harmonics at the expense of temporal resolution. The Universal Short-Time Fourier Transform (U-STFT) resolves this trade-off sequentially by modeling the analysis window duration as a data-adaptive state variable that indexes the number of hops included in the current observation interval. At each frame, a bank of candidate window durations is scored using normalized order-three R\'enyi entropy to quantify joint time-frequency concentration. A window length trellis aggregates the resulting $\mathcal{O}(3^M)$ candidate window schedules with linear complexity per frame, guaranteeing a cumulative mix-loss regret bound of $\mathcal{O}((k+1)\log M)$ relative to any hindsight window schedule with $k$ resolution changes over $M$ frames. By linearity of the Fourier transform, posterior expectation across the candidate bank yields a single spectrum equivalent to an STFT evaluated with a data-adaptive effective window, while an envelope-normalized synthesis stream guarantees exact overlap-add reconstruction. Evaluations on synthetic and marine bioacoustic signals demonstrate adaptive resolution tracking, enhanced spectral concentration, and exact time-domain invertibility.
item.dc:creator: Manan Mittal, Kanad Sarkar, Ryan M. Corey, John R. Buck, Andrew C. Singer

item.title: Doppler-Shannon Association in Vehicular Networks: A Stochastic Geometry Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.37928v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Historically, in cellular networks, the user equipment (UE) association with a base station (BS) has been largely confined to nearest BS association strategies. Unlike cellular networks wherein the BSs are static, vehicular networks are prone to high mobility, resulting in the UE experiencing a Doppler shift. The Doppler shift further results in the fading channel exhibiting high temporal variability. In this work, we present a novel stochastic geometry framework, modeling the effects of the Doppler shift on the physical layer network performance through the coherence time. First, the statistics of the Doppler shift are studied in a two- and three-dimensional Poisson point process (PPP) setting. The distribution and the geometric factors influencing the Doppler shift are analyzed. Next, we propose Doppler shift aware utilities, modeling the Doppler shift induced Shannon rate achievable in time-selective fading links. Through these utilities, we analytically study the outage and coverage probabilities for a UE to achieve a given quality of service. These probabilities are computed based on the optimal BS association in vehicular networks, which goes beyond the closest Euclidean distance. In the UE-BS line of sight, the novel BS association policies factor the BS direction of motion and the fading gain, in addition to the Euclidean distance. We show that the nearest BS is no longer the optimal BS association, resulting in non-convex coverage tessellations associated with the BSs. Our analytical and simulation results illustrate the need for a Doppler shift correction, complementing the ideal SNR based Shannon performance. The network performance achieved through the proposed Doppler-Shannon based association is proved, analytically as well as through simulations, to be superior to the classical Shannon based association.
item.dc:creator: Ashutosh Balakrishnan, Francois Baccelli, Sanjoy Kumar Jhawar, Philippe Martins

item.title: Neuroscience of Improvisation Across Music and Other Domains: A Survey and Outlook
item.description: arXiv:2610.37958v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Improvisation (or Improv), the real-time generation of novel, context-appropriate action, occurs in music, dance, theater, sport, education, therapy, and professional practice. Its neuroscience, however, has been studied almost exclusively for music, where most quantitative neuroimaging evidence lies. A PRISMA-style search done by authors quantifies this imbalance: of 111 identified studies, 70.3\% concern musical improvisation or general psychometric creativity. This explains why earlier surveys are either music-centered or confined to a single construct. This survey addresses that gap in two ways. First, for music, it organizes findings from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), electroencephalography (EEG), functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), hyperscanning, neurofeedback, and brain stimulation, and reports transparently where the evidence agrees (e.g., experience-dependent changes in frontal engagement, increased frontal alpha and theta power) and where it is heterogeneous (e.g., the direction of lateral prefrontal activity, hemispheric lateralization, the interpretation of alpha power). Second, it extends the review to dance, theater, sport, education, therapy, and professional practice, where behavioral, qualitative, and simulation-based studies predominate. Overall, the current evidence does not point to a universal neural signature of improvisation within music domain or other domains. We conclude with an outlook on wearable EEG--fNIRS sensing and closed-loop brain--computer interfaces for musical improvisation, the domain with sufficient evidence, formulated as an expertise-gated control problem and discussed as a possible complement to deliberate practice, and we list the evidence needed for other domains.
item.dc:creator: Levina Perzhilla, Muhammad Mahboob Ur Rahman, Tareq Y. Al-Naffouri

item.title: A Subsample Time-Delay Estimator with a Farrow Structure
item.description: arXiv:2610.37980v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A novel solution to the classical problem of subsample time-delay estimation (TDE) for a wideband signal received by two adjacent sensors is described. A mean squared-error (MSE) measure of dissimilarity is defined and evaluated using a variable fractional-delay (VFD) filter bank with a finite impulse response (FIR). Using a filter bank with a Farrow structure allows the MSE power to be expressed as a polynomial function of the filter delay with a local minimum at the unknown signal delay. In Monte-Carlo simulations, the proposed estimator outperforms the generalized cross-correlation (GCC) technique when the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is not low (less than 10 dB).
item.dc:creator: Hugh L. Kennedy

item.title: Forward-Backward Map Matching for Airborne Magnetic Anomaly Navigation
item.description: arXiv:2610.38047v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Airborne magnetic anomaly navigation provides a passive, unjammable alternative to Global Navigation Satellite Systems positioning by matching magnetometer measurements against a lithospheric magnetic anomaly map. Existing map-matching algorithms either assume a Gaussian posterior (extended Kalman filter), require Monte Carlo sampling (particle filter), or discard posterior uncertainty in favour of a single optimal path (Viterbi algorithm). Here we formulate map matching as inference on a chain-structured factor graph and solve it segment by segment using the forward-backward algorithm, which yields a discrete posterior over candidate positions and its Shannon entropy $H_t$ at time $t$. Over the \texttt{Renfrew\_395} map, $10^3$ synthetic trials yield a median position error of $32.7$ m, $91\%$ below the median inertial drift of $362$ m. On these trials and $10^3$ flight paths, the median error is $43\%$ below the extended Kalman filter and particle filter. Across these paths, a threshold on segment-level entropy detects $47\%$ of segments with errors above two map cells and $94\%$ of those above three, at a $10\%$ false-alarm rate. The foregoing results indicate that $H_t$ provides a truth-free diagnostic of map-conditioned navigation ambiguity.
